The diagonals of a square increase in length at a rate of $1.5\text{ mm/min}.$ At what rate is the area of the square changing when the diagonals are $4\,\text{mm}$ long?
question.worked_solution:
Let $A$ be the area of the square, and $h$ be the length of the diagonal. The relationship between $A$ and $h$ is

$$
A=\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}h}(\frac{{h}^{2}}{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}\cdot h.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that each diagonal of the square is increasing at a rate of $1.5\,\text{mm/min},$ so we have 

$$
\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}=1.5.
$$

Also, when the diagonals are $4\,\text{mm},$ we have $h=4.$ Substituting this information into the above expression for $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}=1.5\cdot 4=6{\text{ mm}}^{2}\text{/min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the area of the square increases at $6\,{\text{mm}}^{2}/\text{min}.$
